sources.claim: A C module boundary places stable public declarations and documented contracts in a header and keeps private helpers and representations inside source files.

canonicalExplanation.summary: A **module** is a header (the public promise) plus a .c file (the private implementation). The header should hold only what callers need: types they use, function prototypes, and **documented contracts** (who owns what, what NULL means, error returns), wrapped in an **include guard**. Everything else stays in the .c file: helper functions marked `static`, and ideally even the struct's layout. An **opaque type** (`typedef struct Stack Stack;` with no body in the header) lets callers hold `Stack *` pointers but never touch the fields, so you can change the representation without breaking them. A good header also **includes what it needs** itself, so it compiles on its own.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner puts the whole stack implementation (struct fields, helper functions and all) into stack.h. Two .c files include it, and the build fails with duplicate definitions. When it's fixed, other code starts poking `s->items` directly, and changing the representation breaks everything. A stack header declares an incomplete struct Stack and public functions while stack.c defines representation and private resize helpers. In this lesson you'll create a self-contained header and matching implementation for a small module.

```predict
{"question": "With `typedef struct Stack Stack;` (no body) in the header, can main.c read s->len?", "options": ["Yes", "No: the struct is incomplete there, so only pointers and the public functions work"], "answer": 1, "why": "That's the point: callers depend on the interface, not the layout."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Failure-safe cleanup**, **Scope, linkage and storage duration**, **Declarations, prototypes and definitions** and **Type aliases and API clarity**.

sections.heading: The rule: public promise in .h, private details in .c
What goes where

includes: Put public types, prototypes and documented contracts in a guarded, self-contained header.
Keep representations and static helpers in the .c file, using opaque types.
excludes: Building and linking multiple files (next lessons).

outcomes: Create a self-contained header and matching implementation for a small module.

examples.title: A stack with a hidden inside
examples.situation: A stack header declares an incomplete struct Stack and public functions while stack.c defines representation and private resize helpers.
walkthrough: **A stack header declares an incomplete struct Stack:** typedef struct Stack Stack; with no body.
**And public functions:** create, destroy, push, pop and size, each with its ownership and error contract.
**stack.c defines representation and private resize helpers:** struct Stack and static grow live only there; switching to a linked list later will not break any caller.
examples.result: Callers use a clean interface, and the implementation can change freely.

examples.title: The header that needed friends
examples.situation: main.c compiles, but test.c fails with "unknown type name 'bool'" when it includes stack.h first.
walkthrough: stack.h used bool without including stdbool.h.
main.c happened to include it earlier, hiding the bug.
Add the needed includes to stack.h; test with a file that includes only it.
examples.result: The header works in any include order.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Every function and structure definition should be placed in a header so all source files can share it.
misconceptions.correction: Headers are pasted into every includer, so definitions there get duplicated and expose private details. Headers declare; one .c file defines.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, why did the build report duplicate definitions?

analogy.example: A module is like **a vending machine**. The header is **the front panel**: buttons, prices, "out of stock returns your money". The .c file is **the inside**: gears and stock layout, locked away. Customers can't reach in (opaque type), so the owner can rearrange the inside without retraining anyone.
limitations: Vending machines rarely change panels; headers should change even less.
The contract printed on the panel is the documentation.

nearTransfer.prompt: Split a single-file counter program into counter.h (opaque Counter, create/increment/get/destroy) and counter.c. Prove the header is self-contained with a file that includes only it.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a queue module with an opaque type, documented contracts for every function (NULL, empty, allocation failure), private helpers and tests. Then change its internal representation and show no caller needs changes.
scaffold: Tests use only the public API.

remediation.explanation: For each item ask: **does a caller need this to use the module?** Yes: header, with a documented contract. No: .c file, static if it's a function.

recap.summary: To create a self-contained module, put only public types, prototypes and documented ownership and error contracts in a guarded header that includes what it needs, keep representations and static helpers in the .c file, and use opaque types so callers can't depend on the layout.
